title: User Input
summary: Read what the user types, and survive the two ways it goes wrong.
refresher: To read what someone types, you need a Scanner. Put `import java.util.Scanner;` at the top of the **file**, then build one with `Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);`. Ask it for the type you want: `nextInt()` for a whole number, `nextDouble()` for a decimal, `nextLine()` for a whole line of text. The catch is that `nextInt()` and `nextDouble()` read the number and stop, leaving the rest of the line unread. A `nextLine()` straight after one of them picks up that leftover and hands you an empty **string**.

sections.title: Scanner basics
sections.summary: Create a Scanner and choose the method that matches the value you need.

blocks.body: A program that asks the user a question does not know the answer ahead of time. In Java, `Scanner` reads typed input. First **import** it. Then create a Scanner connected to the keyboard.

blocks.caption: `System.in` is the keyboard. You hand it to the Scanner once, and from then on `sc` is the **object** you ask for **input**. Notice the prompt uses `print` and not `println`, so the cursor stays on the same line as the question. That is why the greeting appears right after the colon.

blocks.title: Forgetting the import
blocks.body: Leave out `import java.util.Scanner;` and the compiler stops with "cannot find symbol" pointing at the word `Scanner`. It is not saying Scanner does not exist. It is saying you never told it where to look. The **import** line goes above the `class` line, at the very top of the **file**.

From here on the examples show only the statements inside `main`. Assume the **class** wrapper and the **import** are still there, because they always have to be. One more thing to get used to: you do not read input in general. You read a specific type, and you pick the **method** that matches it.

sections.title: Read the right type
sections.summary: Use nextInt, nextDouble, and nextLine intentionally.

blocks.title: The reading methods, and what each one gives back
items: `nextInt()` reads one whole number and gives you an `int`.
`nextDouble()` reads one decimal number and gives you a `double`.
`nextLine()` reads everything up to the end of the line and gives you a `String`.
`next()` reads a single word, stopping at the first space.

blocks.caption: Two numbers of different types, read with the matching **method**. The last line prints 42.0 rather than 42, because a `double` times an `int` is a `double`. Java keeps the more precise type.
blocks.output:
GPA: Credits: GPA 3.5 over 12 credits
Points: 42.0

blocks.title: The wrong method is caught before the program runs
blocks.body: `nextLine()` returns a String. `int age = sc.nextLine();` does not compile because Java will not store text in an int. Convert the text first when you need a number.

sections.title: The leftover newline trap
sections.summary: Handle the Enter key left behind before reading a full line.

blocks.body: Here is the common Scanner trap. `nextInt()` reads the number but leaves the Enter key behind as a newline. The next `nextLine()` reads that leftover newline and returns an empty **string**. Add an extra `nextLine()` when you need to clear it.

blocks.caption: The fix is one throwaway `sc.nextLine();` whose only job is to consume the leftover newline. You ignore what it returns. In the broken version the program does not even stop at the Name prompt, and that is the tell: if a prompt flashes past without waiting, an unread newline is why.

blocks.prompt: The user types 90, presses Enter, types Great work, and presses Enter. What does this **print**?
blocks.why: `nextInt()` takes the 90 and stops, leaving the newline from that first Enter unread. `nextLine()` then reads to the end of that same line, which is nothing at all, so `comment` is the empty **string** and the brackets **print** with nothing between them. The words Great work are still waiting on the next line, unread. Put a bare `sc.nextLine();` between the two lines and the comment arrives.

sections.title: Invalid input symptoms
sections.summary: Recognize what happens when typed text cannot become the requested type.

blocks.body: `next()` reads one word and stops before the rest of the line. If the user types `Ada Lovelace`, `next()` gives `Ada`, and a later `nextLine()` may read ` Lovelace`. Each reading method leaves unused text for the next method.

blocks.caption: The user typed the word twelve at a prompt that called `nextInt()`. Java cannot turn that into an `int`, so it throws an InputMismatchException and the program stops there. The line `You typed` never prints. This is a **runtime error**: the code compiled fine, and only the actual **input** broke it.
blocks.output: How many credits? Exception in thread "main" java.util.InputMismatchException

blocks.title: A crash on input is not a crash in your code
blocks.body: InputMismatchException usually means Java expected a number but read something else. First check whether your prompts and Scanner calls read the values in the same order the user types them.

blocks.prompt: The user types 2, a space, then 3, and presses Enter. What does this **print**?
choices: It crashes, because two numbers on one line need two Enters
blocks.why: Both `nextInt()` calls work, and they read across the space happily, so `a` is 2 and `b` is 3. The trap is the last line. Java works left to right, and `"Sum: " + a` is a **String** joined to a number, which produces the String `"Sum: 2"`. Joining 3 to that gives `"Sum: 23"`. This joining is called **concatenation**. The `+` only adds when both sides are numbers; once a String is involved it joins text instead. To get 5, do the arithmetic in its own parentheses: `"Sum: " + (a + b)`.

sections.title: Input habits
sections.summary: Use input rules that keep beginner programs readable and safer.

blocks.title: Working rules for reading input
items: **Import** `java.util.Scanner` and create the Scanner once, near the top of `main`. One Scanner for the whole program is enough.
Prompt before every read, with `print` rather than `println`, so the user knows what you are waiting for.
Match the **method** to the type: `nextInt()` for `int`, `nextDouble()` for `double`, `nextLine()` for `String`.
After any `nextInt()`, `nextDouble()`, or `next()`, put a bare `sc.nextLine();` before your next `nextLine()`.
If a prompt appears but the program does not stop and wait, an unread newline is the reason.
If you get an InputMismatchException, compare the order you are reading **values** in against the order the user types them.

user-input-lesson-check-1.title: Typed values start as text
user-input-lesson-check-1.body: User input enters the program as text first. Convert it before doing arithmetic.
user-input-lesson-check-1.notice: Text addition joins characters. Numeric addition adds quantities.
user-input-lesson-check-1.mistake: Do not calculate with raw input when the value is meant to be a number.

user-input-lesson-check-2.title: Invalid numbers need a response
user-input-lesson-check-2.body: If the program asks for a number and receives words or blank text, conversion can fail. Plan what the user should do next.
user-input-lesson-check-2.notice: Validation is part of input handling, not an optional extra after the calculation.
user-input-lesson-check-2.mistake: Do not continue as if a failed conversion produced a useful number.

user-input-summary-01.title: Input is outside data
user-input-summary-01.body: Anything a person types should be treated as outside text until the program checks and converts it.
user-input-summary-01.notice: The program has to decide whether the typed value is text, a whole number, or a decimal.
user-input-summary-01.mistake: Do not assume a value is numeric just because the prompt asked for a number.

user-input-supplement-01.title: Raw input joins like text
user-input-supplement-01.body: When two typed values are still strings, `+` does **concatenation**, which means joining the characters end to end. Convert first when the assignment asks for a total.
user-input-supplement-01.notice: The same symbol can join strings or add numbers depending on the value types.
user-input-supplement-01.mistake: Do not let numeric-looking strings fool you into skipping conversion.

user-input-authored-01.title: Know the input type
user-input-authored-01.body: Before using an input value, identify what type the input function returns in your language.
user-input-authored-01.notice: A typed value may look like a number while still being stored as text.
user-input-authored-01.mistake: Do not mix raw input with numeric code until the type is clear.

user-input-authored-02.title: Conversion can fail
user-input-authored-02.body: Numeric conversion only works when the text has the right shape for the target number type.
user-input-authored-02.notice: Words, blanks, and extra symbols can make conversion fail.
user-input-authored-02.mistake: Do not treat every bad input as a logic error later in the program.

user-input-authored-03.title: Ask text or number first
user-input-authored-03.body: The first design question for input is simple: should this value stay text, or does the next step need a quantity?
user-input-authored-03.notice: The correct choice depends on how the value will be used next.
user-input-authored-03.mistake: Do not convert names, yes/no words, or labels just because they came from input.

user-input-authored-04.title: Some answers should stay strings
user-input-authored-04.body: Names, course codes, yes/no answers, and messages usually stay as text unless arithmetic or numeric ordering is needed.
user-input-authored-04.notice: Text comparison and numeric comparison answer different questions.
user-input-authored-04.mistake: Do not convert a value if conversion would remove meaning, such as leading zeroes or letters.

user-input-authored-05.title: Convert quantities before using them
user-input-authored-05.body: Counts, scores, prices, credits, and temperatures usually need numeric conversion before calculations.
user-input-authored-05.notice: Convert once, store the converted value, then calculate with that clear value.
user-input-authored-05.mistake: Do not repeatedly convert the same raw text in several different places.

user-input-authored-06.title: Prompts should be readable
user-input-authored-06.body: A prompt is part of the user interface. Leave enough spacing and wording so the person knows what kind of answer to type.
user-input-authored-06.notice: Good prompt text reduces input mistakes before validation even runs.
user-input-authored-06.mistake: Do not hide the expected value type from the person using the program.
